q: A wall is replaced by one of the same material and area but twice as thick. The temperature difference is unchanged. The rate of conduction becomes
why: $\Delta Q/\Delta t = -kA\,\Delta T/\Delta x$: doubling $\Delta x$ halves the temperature gradient, so the rate halves.

q: How much energy, in kJ, heats 2.0 kg of water by 5.0 K? Take $c = 4200\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$.
why: $Q = mc\Delta T = 2.0 \times 4200 \times 5.0 = 42\,000$ J $= 42$ kJ.

q: Ice melts at a constant 0 °C while energy is supplied. The energy mainly increases
options: the average kinetic energy of the molecules
the mean speed of the molecules
why: Temperature is constant, so the average kinetic energy is constant; the energy goes into separating molecules, raising their potential energy.

q: How much energy, in kJ, melts 0.50 kg of ice already at 0 °C? Take $L_f = 3.3 \times 10^{5}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$.
why: $Q = mL = 0.50 \times 3.3 \times 10^{5} = 1.65 \times 10^{5}$ J $= 165$ kJ. No $\Delta T$: melting happens at constant temperature.

q: The absolute temperature of a black body doubles and its surface area stays the same. Its luminosity is multiplied by
why: $L = \sigma A T^4$, so $L \propto T^4$ and $2^4 = 16$.

q: A star's spectrum peaks at 500 nm. Treating it as a black body, its surface temperature is about
Why is the mean incoming solar intensity over the whole Earth $S/4$?
options: Earth's albedo reflects three quarters of it
The atmosphere absorbs three quarters of it
Only a quarter of Earth faces the Sun at any time
Earth's surface area is four times its cross-sectional area
why: Power is intercepted by the disc $\pi R^2$ but spread over the sphere $4\pi R^2$. Half of Earth (not a quarter) is lit at any time.

q: Take the solar constant as $1360\ \text{W m}^{-2}$. What is the mean incoming intensity over the whole Earth, in $\text{W m}^{-2}$?
why: Mean intensity $= S/4 = 1360/4 = 340\ \text{W m}^{-2}$.

q: Mean incoming intensity is $340\ \text{W m}^{-2}$ and Earth's albedo is 0.30. What intensity is absorbed, in $\text{W m}^{-2}$?
why: A fraction $1 - 0.30 = 0.70$ is absorbed: $0.70 \times 340 = 238\ \text{W m}^{-2}$.

q: Greenhouse gases warm the Earth mainly by absorbing
why: The atmosphere is mostly transparent to incoming visible light; greenhouse gases absorb the infrared re-emitted by the warm surface and re-radiate it in all directions.

q: Which of these is not one of the main greenhouse gases?
why: Nitrogen (N<sub>2</sub>) makes up most of the atmosphere but barely absorbs infrared. Nitrous oxide (N<sub>2</sub>O) is a greenhouse gas: don't mix them up.

q: Polar ice melts, exposing darker sea. This causes further warming because Earth's
why: Dark sea reflects less than ice, so albedo falls and more incoming radiation is absorbed. The solar constant depends on the Sun, not on Earth.

q: An ideal gas at constant volume is heated from 27 °C to 327 °C. Its pressure
why: Use kelvin: 300 K to 600 K doubles $T$, so $P$ doubles. Using °C gives the wrong ratio $327/27 \approx 12$.

q: An ideal gas at 150 kPa is compressed from 2.0 L to 0.50 L at constant temperature. What is the new pressure, in kPa?
why: $P_1V_1 = P_2V_2$: the volume is quartered, so the pressure is multiplied by 4: $4 \times 150 = 600$ kPa.

q: In the kinetic model, the pressure of a gas is caused by
options: the change of momentum of molecules hitting the walls
why: Each wall collision reverses the molecule's momentum component, so the wall exerts a force on it (and it on the wall). Ideal gas molecules have no intermolecular forces.

q: The kelvin temperature of an ideal gas is doubled. The square root of the mean squared speed of its molecules, $\sqrt{\overline{v^2}}$, is multiplied by
why: Mean kinetic energy $\tfrac{1}{2}m\overline{v^2} \propto T$, so $\overline{v^2}$ doubles and $\sqrt{\overline{v^2}}$ goes up by $\sqrt{2}$, not 2.

q: A real gas behaves most like an ideal gas at
why: Low pressure (low density) means molecules are far apart, so their volume and intermolecular forces matter little; high temperature keeps it far from liquefying.

q: What is the internal energy, in kJ, of 2.0 mol of a monatomic ideal gas at 300 K? Take $R = 8.31\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$.
why: $U = \tfrac{3}{2}nRT = 1.5 \times 2.0 \times 8.31 \times 300 \approx 7480$ J $\approx 7.5$ kJ. An ideal gas has no potential energy, only kinetic.

q: A gas absorbs 500 J of thermal energy and does 200 J of work on its surroundings. What is its change in internal energy, in J?
why: $Q = \Delta U + W$, so $\Delta U = 500 - 200 = 300$ J. Work done by the gas is positive.

q: What is the Carnot efficiency of an engine working between reservoirs at 400 K and 300 K?
why: $\eta = 1 - T_c/T_h = 1 - 300/400 = 0.25$. 0.75 is $T_c/T_h$ alone; 0.33 divides by the cold temperature.

q: An ideal gas expands adiabatically. Which is correct?
why: Adiabatic means $Q = 0$, so $\Delta U = -W$. The gas does positive work, so $U$ and hence $T$ fall. Constant temperature would be isothermal.

q: A gas expands at a constant pressure of 200 kPa from $0.010\ \text{m}^3$ to $0.025\ \text{m}^3$. How much work does it do, in J?
why: $W = P\Delta V = 2.0 \times 10^{5} \times 0.015 = 3000$ J. Remember to convert kPa to Pa.

q: A fridge lowers the entropy of the food inside it. Why does this not break the second law?
options: The fridge is an isolated system
Energy is conserved in the process
The entropy of the surroundings rises by at least as much
why: Entropy can fall locally in a non-isolated system if the surroundings gain at least as much. Energy conservation is the first law, not the second.

q: A large reservoir at 300 K receives 600 J of thermal energy. Its entropy change, in $\text{J K}^{-1}$, is
why: $\Delta S = \Delta Q/T = 600/300 = 2.0\ \text{J K}^{-1}$. Its temperature barely changes, but its entropy still rises: it is $\Delta Q/T$, not $\Delta T$, that matters. 0.5 is $T/Q$ the wrong way up.

q: A current of 3.0 A flows for 20 s. How much charge passes, in C?
why: $\Delta q = I\Delta t = 3.0 \times 20 = 60$ C.

q: What is the total resistance of a 4.0 Ω and a 12 Ω resistor in parallel?
why: $1/R = 1/4 + 1/12 = 4/12$, so $R = 3.0$ Ω. 0.33 forgets to take the reciprocal; 16 Ω is the series value.

q: A wire is replaced by one of the same metal with twice the length and twice the diameter. Its resistance is
why: $R = \rho L/A$. Doubling the diameter makes the area 4 times larger, so $R \propto 2/4 = 1/2$.

q: A cell of emf 12 V and internal resistance 1.0 Ω is connected to a 5.0 Ω resistor. What is the terminal potential difference, in V?
why: $I = \varepsilon/(R + r) = 12/6.0 = 2.0$ A, so the terminal pd is $IR = 2.0 \times 5.0 = 10$ V (2 V is lost inside the cell).

q: The light shining on a light-dependent resistor (LDR) gets brighter. Its resistance
why: More light frees more charge carriers in the LDR, so its resistance falls, but never to zero.

q: The potential difference across a fixed resistor is halved. The power dissipated becomes
why: $P = V^2/R$, so halving $V$ gives $(1/2)^2 = 1/4$ of the power. The current also halves, which is why it isn't one half.
